title: Mass of a biodegradable condensation copolymer from glycine and 6-aminohexanoic acid
summary: Five short screens: charge the reactor, watch CH3I become glycine one reagent at a time, watch caprolactam's ring unroll into 6-aminohexanoic acid, link the two monomers while every condensation ejects a water, assemble the arithmetic - and then reveal the mass of Z in spray-paint lettering.
subject: Chemistry
topic: Condensation copolymer from a reaction sequence
subtopics: Hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid
Acidic hydrolysis of a lactam and ring opening
Condensation polymerisation and the water eliminated
Linear chain: n units give n minus 1 links
concepts: Cyanide displacement is the only step in the sequence that changes the carbon count, which alone fixes X as a two-carbon acid
Red P with Br2 is the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction and brominates the alpha carbon of an acid
Excess ammonia converts an alpha-bromo acid to an alpha-amino acid without alkylating twice
A lactam is a cyclic amide; hydrolysis adds a water across the C-N bond and opens the ring, so the product is 18 heavier than the lactam
A polyamide needs an amine at one end and an acid at the other, which is why both monomers must be acyclic
Condensation polymerisation ejects one small molecule per link, so the polymer is always lighter than the monomers that made it
A chain of n units with two loose ends has n minus 1 links, not n - the word acyclic in the question is what makes it 999 rather than 1000
Not every number given in a question is used: bromine appears only in an intermediate and never reaches the answer
formulas: R-X + CN- gives R-CN, one carbon longer
R-CN with H3O+ and heat gives R-COOH
red P / Br2 = HVZ: alpha-bromination of a carboxylic acid
alpha-bromo acid + excess NH3 gives an alpha-amino acid
lactam + H2O gives the amino acid (ring opens)
links = total monomer units - number of chains
mass of polymer = sum of monomer masses - links x 18

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: both structures, both molar masses, the link count and the arithmetic were fixed independently

The carbon count tracked through the whole sequence: CH3I has one carbon and glycine has two, and the only step that adds carbon is the cyanide displacement, which alone forces X to be a two-carbon acid independently of recognising the reagents
Hydrolysis of the lactam checked atom by atom rather than by name: C6H11NO + H2O = C6H13NO2 balances on every element, and 113 + 18 = 131 on the masses

The answer computed twice by different routes: subtracting the water from the monomer mass gives 85018 g, and counting the atoms of one mole of chain (C4000 H7002 N1000 O1001) and multiplying by the atomic masses gives 85018 g to machine precision
Conservation of mass checked explicitly: 103000 g of monomer = 85018 g of polymer + 17982 g of water, with no element going negative

The model tested away from the paper's numbers: two chains instead of one gives 85036 g, a 300/700 split gives 96218 g, and with one unit per chain no links form, no water is lost and the mass reduces to the monomer mass - so the formula degrades correctly at the boundary rather than by luck
The distractors reproduced deliberately: losing 1000 waters gives 85000; forgetting the water gives 103000; using caprolactam (113) in place of Y gives 94000. None is 85018

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which identifies the same X and Y, uses the same 999 waters and reports the same 85018. IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable at the time of writing

Headless-browser run of the finished page: 98 assertions driving the whole flow - the chemistry the page is built on, the model's behaviour away from the paper's numbers, the empty control panel with the answer nowhere on it, the refusal of more chains than units, each of the four experiment screens in turn (the four reagent steps with the right molecule on screen, the ring opening with water attacking the C-N bond, one water per link accelerating to 999, and the arithmetic with its last value withheld), the suspense card, the graffiti reveal with its spray filter and particle burst, the header blinking once and stopping, the record and monomer cards, a re-run on different data giving a different answer, replay, theme toggle, clean console, zero horizontal overflow at 390 px and 360 px, and a theatre that fits in one window
verification.note: The paper says 500 mol of X and 500 mol of Y, not 500 mL; the simulation quotes it as the paper does and takes amounts in moles. IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable; the published solution used for cross-checking agrees on both monomers, on the 999 waters and on the final number.

interactivity: Five short screens following one principle - enter the data, watch the chemistry, see the numbers, reveal the answer - with the whole run taking about forty seconds

A reactor control panel with three glass vessels: how much X, how much Y, and how many moles of polymer they must end up as, with the atomic masses underneath, pre-filled from the question and editable
Every molar mass on the page is summed from those four atomic masses, so nothing is a remembered constant and changing carbon to 13 changes every number downstream
Bromine is shown in the panel but greyed out and labelled as never reaching the answer - a number the question gives that is not a number you use
Nothing is identified at the start: the panel does not say what X and Y are, and the reactor works them out
The reactor refuses a charge it cannot make - more chains than monomer units - with the reason given against the field

Screen 2 builds X from CH3I with the four reagents flying in one at a time, the molecule redrawn at each step and only the group that changed haloed, with a five-stop rail tracking CH3I to CH3CN to CH3COOH to BrCH2COOH to the amino acid
Each step is named as it happens: cyanide displacement, nitrile hydrolysis, Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky, ammonolysis

Screen 3 draws caprolactam as a real seven-membered ring with the C-N bond about to break picked out in red, sends a water molecule in to attack it, and then unrolls the ring into a zig-zag chain - the same seven atoms morphing from heptagon to chain while H2N appears at one end and OH grows at the other
The ring-opening screen shows 113 + 18 = 131 as it finishes, so the molar mass of Y is seen to come from the chemistry

Screen 4 feeds two streams of monomers into a reactor, grows the chain one unit at a time alternating the two colours, and ejects a visible water molecule at every link while live counters show units linked, links formed and water released
After six links the animation accelerates smoothly to 1000 units and 999 waters - the water count staying one behind the unit count, which is the whole question
Screen 5 assembles the arithmetic one line at a time and deliberately withholds the last value, leaving 103 000 minus 17 982 equals a question mark
A suspense card then asks what the mass of Z is, over a row of blanks, with a pulsing Reveal answer button
The reveal sprays the answer across the screen in rough-edged graffiti lettering with drips, an offset shadow and a burst of particles and chemical glyphs, and the header answer box blinks once
Reference cards for both monomers are drawn afterwards with their molar masses added up element by element from the atomic masses entered
Replay experiment and change the data are available from every screen after the first, and the entries are kept

Four cards on the wrong answers this question really produces: 85000 from losing 1000 waters, 103000 from forgetting the water, 94000 from using caprolactam as Y, and getting stuck hunting for bromine
A record of the run that fills in quantity by quantity, and the derivation gated until the answer is revealed
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log
